title: Erik Prince Team Pitched White House on El Salvador Detention Camp Plan
description_short: Politico reported that Erik Prince’s team pitched a proposed El Salvador detention and deportation operation; no approval was established.
description_medium: Politico reported on April 11, 2025, that former Blackwater chief Erik Prince and defense contractors pitched the White House on a plan involving a 10,000-person detention camp and transportation for as many as 100,000 people. The article describes a proposal, not an approved contract or an operating program, and says White House interest was unclear.
description_long: On April 11, 2025, POLITICO reported that former Blackwater chief Erik Prince and defense contractors were pitching the White House on a proposal connected to deportations to El Salvador. The proposal described gathering as many as 100,000 people from U.S. prisons, holding them in a 10,000-person detention camp, and flying them to El Salvador. It said Prince’s group, partnering with El Salvador, would handle the logistics and would need access to government immigration files held by law-enforcement agencies to determine people’s immigration status. The proposal claimed a contract would help resolve legal issues and improve the government’s ability to locate, capture, detain, and deport immigrants; those were claims in the pitch, not legal findings. An administration official expected the proposal to be discussed during Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele’s planned White House visit. Prince and the White House declined to comment. POLITICO also reported that an LLC called 2USV was registered in Wyoming, which the article described as an indication that Prince’s group hoped to move to a more serious phase of pitching. The report describes proposed terms and a contractor pitch; it does not report an awarded contract or say the camp or flights began.

It directed DHS to develop a uniform policy making federal law-enforcement personnel clearly identifiable, increased funding for DHS’s Office of Inspector General by $37 million, a 20 percent increase, and provided funding for the Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties and the Office of the Citizenship and Immigration Services Ombudsman. The congressional release said the action would restart federal employees’ paychecks and allow services, including FEMA disaster response and Coast Guard operations, to resume.

title: Trump Orders Increased Transfers of Federal Assets to Local Police
description_short: Executive Order 14288 directs an increase in transfers of excess federal military and national-security assets to local law enforcement.
description_medium: On April 28, 2025, President Donald Trump issued Executive Order 14288, directing the Attorney General and Defense Secretary to increase provision of excess military and national-security assets to state and local law enforcement within 90 days. It also orders a review of covered police consent decrees. A July opinion column relayed the Legal Defense Fund’s concerns about aggressive policing and accountability; completed transfers and effects were not established.
description_long: On April 28, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14288, “Strengthening and Unleashing America’s Law Enforcement to Pursue Criminals and Protect Innocent Citizens.” The order directs the Attorney General and Secretary of Defense, consulting the Secretary of Homeland Security and other appropriate agency heads, to increase the provision of excess military and national-security assets to state and local law enforcement within 90 days. It also directs Defense, coordinating with the Attorney General, to determine how assets, training, non-lethal capabilities and personnel could be used to prevent crime. Separately, the Attorney General is directed to review covered police consent decrees and related measures and modify, rescind or seek to conclude those judged to unduly impede law-enforcement functions. These are agency directives, rather than a record of completed transfers or concluded decrees. A July 2025 Times-Republican opinion column relayed the Legal Defense Fund’s concerns that the order could promote aggressive policing and make accountability more difficult. The column’s concerns describe potential effects rather than documented misconduct.

title: Eleventh Circuit Holds Boca Raton and Palm Beach County Conversion-Therapy Ordinances Violate the First Amendment
description_short: A divided Eleventh Circuit panel held that conversion-therapy ordinances in Boca Raton and Palm Beach County violated the First Amendment.
description_medium: On November 20, 2020, a divided Eleventh Circuit panel ruled in Otto v. City of Boca Raton that ordinances in Boca Raton and Palm Beach County restricting licensed therapists from providing sexual-orientation-change counseling to minors violated the First Amendment. The court treated the rules as content-based speech regulations that failed strict scrutiny. Judge Beverly Martin dissented.
description_long: On November 20, 2020, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit decided an appeal by licensed therapists Robert Otto and Julie Hamilton challenging ordinances adopted by the City of Boca Raton and Palm Beach County. The local rules restricted licensed therapists from providing sexual-orientation-change counseling to minors. The City’s ordinance exempted clergy and allowed supportive counseling for people undergoing gender transition. The majority held that the ordinances regulated speech based on its content and could not survive strict scrutiny under the First Amendment. It reversed the district court’s denial of a preliminary injunction and remanded for entry of an injunction consistent with the opinion. Judge Beverly Martin dissented, arguing that the ordinances regulated professional conduct. The ruling concerned those two local ordinances and the therapists’ preliminary-injunction appeal; it did not announce a nationwide policy. The official opinion identifies the panel as Martin, Britt Grant, and Barbara Lagoa.

description_short: White House Spanish-Language Website and X Profile Taken Offline in 2025
description_medium: Within hours of Donald Trump’s January 20, 2025 inauguration, the Spanish-language White House website was taken offline and showed a 404 error. An Associated Press report republished by PBS NewsHour also identified the White House’s Spanish-language X profile, @LaCasaBlanca, and a government reproductive-freedom page as disbanded. A White House spokesperson said the site was being edited and said the Spanish translation section would return; the report gave no restoration date.
description_long:
At about 4 p.m. Eastern on January 20, 2025, hours after Donald Trump’s inauguration, the Spanish versions of the White House website and social media accounts became unavailable, according to TrumpFile’s timeline. The Associated Press, in a report republished by PBS NewsHour, said the new administration took down the Spanish-language White House website; the site returned an “Error 404” message. The report named the White House’s Spanish-language X profile, @LaCasaBlanca, and the government page on reproductive freedom as also disbanded. It noted that Spanish pages for the Departments of Labor, Justice, and Agriculture remained available on Tuesday.

Asked about the change on the administration’s second day, principal deputy press secretary Harrison Fields said the White House was developing, editing, and tweaking its website, and that some archived content had gone dormant. He said the administration was committed to bringing the Spanish translation section back online and reloading dormant content “in a short timeline,” without specifying when. The contemporaneous reporting documents the initial outage and the administration’s stated plan; it does not establish a later restoration date or whether every affected page or account returned. The announced restoration commitment did not specify how long the outage would last.

It also recounted users’ wordplay, including one person joking about ordering a grande “covfefe,” while some commenters defended the post as a possible human error. The article noted that Merriam-Webster’s site suggested words such as “coffee,” “coven,” and “cover” when searching for “covfefe.” After deleting the original, Trump posted: “Who can figure out the true meaning of ‘covfefe’ ??? Enjoy!” The follow-up invited speculation but did not explain the original wording. The reporting leaves Trump’s intended word or meaning unresolved.

title: Trump Signs H-1B Proclamation Requiring $100,000 Payment for Certain New Petitions
description_short: Proclamation 10973 conditioned entry for certain H-1B workers on a $100,000 payment; the requirement began September 21, 2025, with exceptions.
description_medium: On September 19, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Proclamation 10973, restricting entry of certain H-1B workers unless a $100,000 payment accompanied the petition. It took effect at 12:01 a.m. EDT on September 21. White House guidance said it covered new petitions and did not change renewal fees.

The proclamation took effect at 12:01 a.m. EDT on September 21, 2025, and set an initial 12-month term absent extension. It directed employers to obtain and retain proof of payment before filing petitions for workers outside the United States, and assigned payment verification and implementation roles to the State and Homeland Security departments. The White House FAQ said the payment applied to new petitions submitted after the effective time, not previously issued visas or earlier petitions, and did not change renewal fees. title: Nine States Had Rejected DOJ Voter-Data Lawsuits by June 2026
description_short: AP reported that courts in nine states had rejected DOJ lawsuits seeking detailed voter-registration data, including Maryland.
description_medium: On June 23, 2026, the Associated Press reported that U.S. District Judge Stephanie Gallagher dismissed the Justice Department’s suit seeking Maryland’s detailed voter records. description_long: The Associated Press reported on June 23, 2026, that U.S. District Judge Stephanie Gallagher dismissed the Justice Department’s suit seeking Maryland’s detailed voter-registration records. Gallagher, appointed by President Donald Trump during his first term, wrote that she “joins every court to have addressed this issue” in concluding that the unredacted voter file was not a record Maryland had to produce to the United States. The Justice Department relied on an opinion from its Office of Legal Counsel asserting a right to the data under federal civil-rights law; Gallagher wrote that the court would not interpret the Civil Rights Act contrary to its text simply because the office advancing that view had adopted it. AP said the records sought included dates of birth, addresses, driver’s-license numbers and partial Social Security numbers. It reported that Maryland brought the number of states where courts had rejected similar demands to nine, and that DOJ had sued in 30 states and the District of Columbia. The AP report also identified similar rulings in Arizona, California, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Oregon, Rhode Island and Wisconsin. It described a Georgia dismissal as based on filing in the wrong city, after which DOJ refiled elsewhere.

description_long:
On November 7, 2019, New York Attorney General Letitia James announced that the New York Supreme Court had ordered Donald Trump to pay $2 million in damages for improperly using charitable assets to advance his political interests during the 2016 presidential primaries. The order formed part of the resolution of the state’s lawsuit against the Trump Foundation and its directors.

Trump admitted personally misusing Foundation funds. The admissions included allowing his campaign to control the timing, amounts and recipients of approximately $2.8 million raised through a January 2016 veterans fundraiser. He also admitted using charitable money to settle obligations of companies he controlled and purchasing a $10,000 portrait with Foundation funds.

The Foundation had agreed to dissolve under court supervision in December 2018. The resolution directed its remaining $1.78 million in assets and Trump’s damages payment to eight independent charities. It required training for the Trump children and imposed restrictions on Trump’s future charitable service, including independent oversight and a five-year reporting requirement if he formed a new charity.

title: Muslim Ban 2.0 — Executive Order 13780
description_short: Executive Order 13780 imposed temporary entry restrictions on nationals of six countries and paused refugee admissions in 2017.
description_medium: On March 6, 2017, Trump signed Executive Order 13780, replacing his first travel order. It directed a 90-day entry suspension for nationals of six countries, with exceptions, and a 120-day refugee pause. Iraq was removed from the covered list. Hawaii and Maryland courts blocked key provisions in separate cases. The Fourth Circuit upheld restrictions on enforcement on constitutional grounds; the Ninth Circuit relied on immigration statutes.
description_long:
On March 6, 2017, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780, replacing his January travel order. It directed a 90-day entry suspension for nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen, subject to exceptions and discretionary waivers. Iraq was removed from the covered-country list. The restriction applied to specified people outside the United States who lacked valid visas at the dates set out in the order. Lawful permanent residents and dual nationals traveling on passports from non-designated countries were among those exempted. A separate provision directed a 120-day suspension of refugee travel and refugee-status decisions, subject to waivers. The scheduled effective date was March 16.

The litigation proceeded through separate cases. Hawaii issued a temporary restraining order against Sections 2 and 6 on March 15, followed by a preliminary injunction on March 29. Maryland enjoined Section 2(c) on March 16. On May 25, the Fourth Circuit substantially upheld the Maryland injunction based on the plaintiffs’ likely success under the Establishment Clause. On June 12, the Ninth Circuit largely upheld the Hawaii injunction on statutory grounds, while narrowing its scope. On June 26, the Supreme Court partly stayed the injunctions, permitting enforcement against people without a credible claim of a bona fide relationship with a person or entity in the United States.

description_short: Trump notified Congress on April 3, 2020, that he intended to remove Michael Atkinson and immediately placed the intelligence inspector general on leave.
description_medium: On April 3, 2020, Trump notified Congress that he intended to remove Intelligence Community Inspector General Michael Atkinson, citing lost confidence. description_long: On April 3, 2020, President Donald Trump placed Intelligence Community Inspector General Michael Atkinson on administrative leave for thirty days pending his removal. Trump’s notification to Congress cited a loss of confidence in Atkinson. A bipartisan group of senators objected that this explanation lacked the details Congress expected under the inspector general removal safeguards. They also questioned whether immediately sidelining Atkinson undermined the required advance notice and Congress’s opportunity to discuss the decision. Atkinson had handled the Ukraine whistleblower complaint that figured in Trump’s first impeachment. After determining that the complaint involved an urgent concern, he forwarded it to the director of national intelligence. When Atkinson and acting Director Joseph Maguire disagreed about sending it to Congress, Atkinson notified lawmakers of that disagreement. Maguire ultimately transmitted the complaint itself. The distinction matters: Atkinson’s role was to assess and report the concern through the oversight process, rather than independently deliver the complaint to Congress. The removal raised questions about watchdog independence, while the senators’ objections constituted oversight criticism rather than a judicial determination that Trump’s action was unlawful.
